text: PRRS is caused by a virus that attacks and destroys macrophages, the cells responsible for catching and destroying microbes entering through the lungs; disease severity is closely tied to secondary bacterial infection and interaction with other viruses like CSF. Transmission: saliva, feces, urine, and colostrum of infected animals; people via shoes/clothes/hands; contaminated injection needles; boar semen; ducks are suspected as a possible vector. Symptoms vary with health status; some strains are 'Highly Pathogenic' with high mortality. In sows (the clearest sign in Cambodia): several sows go off feed for 7–10 days; fever around 40°C (lower than CSF's >41°C); many abortions; farrowing at 108–111 days; weak piglets at birth with many mummified; high maternity mortality, litters reduced to just 2–4 piglets; hard-to-stop diarrhea in suckling piglets; some sow deaths; a minority show blue ears (giving the disease its nickname 'Blue Ear Disease'), though this is rare and not reliable for diagnosis alone. In post-weaning piglets: lung macrophage destruction plus loss of maternal antibody protection causes strong cough and difficult breathing, and a wasting condition with rough coat and exudative dermatitis; mortality is limited with antibiotic treatment for secondary infection, but growth stays poor through fattening. In growing/fattening pigs: fever and coughing (especially where Mycoplasma is already endemic), swollen discharging eyes, sunburn-like skin redness, reduced feed intake and body condition. Disease dynamics: sows/boars shed virus for about 2 weeks, but fattening pigs shed for an average of 2 months; fetuses infected during gestation (especially after day 75), if they survive, shed virus for 5 months and are weak at birth — removing them is recommended, and buying piglets from unknown sources is risky for this reason; post-weaning piglets (with low immunity, no longer protected by maternal antibodies) sustain infection in the farm by picking it up from asymptomatic-shedding fattening pigs. Diagnosis: NaVRI lab testing, though not very sensitive (blood from at least 12 pigs is needed for a reliable result), and it cannot distinguish natural infection from vaccination. Treatment: none directly (viral), but medication reduces impact — lactating sows: long-acting Tetracycline 2 days before farrowing and on the day of farrowing, then Doxycycline mixed in feed for 1 month; pregnant sows: Doxycycline mixed in feed for 6 weeks (injectable long-acting Tetracycline for any not eating); weaning piglets: Florfenicol in creep feed from 1 week before to 2 weeks after weaning; post-weaning/fattening pigs treated symptomatically for respiratory disease and fever. Prevention: biosecurity is the most important tool — limit farm visits (especially by vets and other farmers), require visitors to change clothes/shoes and wash hands, never buy post-weaned piglets from an unknown source, and use separate, clean needles for different pig groups. Vaccination is complicated: PRRS mutates readily with many circulating strains, vaccines cannot control an active mortality outbreak, and since PRRS vaccines are live modified vaccines, vaccinating introduces virus onto the farm that can itself spread and mutate — PRRS vaccine should only be used on already-infected farms to improve newborn piglet survival and reproductive performance, never to control an acute outbreak.
